title: Why Basie took over the Moten band
summary: Edison says Basie was popular and, as a pianist, the logical leader, as pianists often led bands then.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: How do you account for the fact that Basie took that band over, though? I mean, more or less from Moten. I mean, wasn't Basie sort of --
He was very popular in Kansas, Basie was. And --
Well, he wasn't sort of like --

I don't know how he inherited the band but I think he was just a very popular guy, you know. And some guys around there that he knew, like Piney Brown and all those guys, they gave him the name of "Count", you know.
You know, knowing over the years -- well, since I've known him, anyway, it seems strange that he would have taken over a band, you know.
No, well, he was the only logical one to take it over because piano players were bandleaders in those days.
That's right, there was Claude Hopkins.
Yeah, Claude Hopkins, Duke, Earl Hines, Fletcher. That was the piano players era for bands. Except Louie Armstrong. He was always a band leader.

But piano players, well they would seem more likely to have a band because they could sit from the piano, they could direct. You take an instrumentalist, you'd have to hire two of what you were playing. Like if the band leader was a tenor player, they'd have to hire another tenor player. If the band leader was a trumpet player, they'd have to have another one. But the piano player, you wouldn't have to hire nobody else. So automatically, he would become the bandleader, the director, you know.
But Basie was popular around Kansas City.
